body:
A play is written to be performed. The script holds two kinds of text: dialogue, which the characters speak, and stage directions, in parentheses, which tell the actors what to do and the audience what to see.

In a play, nobody explains what a character is thinking. You learn about characters from what they say, what they do, and what they hide.

Playwrights love dramatic irony: when the audience knows something a character does not. Watching a character walk right past the answer is tense, or funny, or both.

This unit we read two original scenes, "The Volcano" and "The Interview." In small groups you will rehearse and perform "The Volcano" as readers' theater, then write about how its dramatic irony works.
title: When the Audience Knows More
